pages.text: Every evening, eleven-year-old Teye played football near the beach with his friends. One Saturday, he arrived with his football and stopped. ‘Where is our goalpost?’ he asked. The wooden posts lay in the sand, almost touching the waves. ‘The sea has stolen our football field!’ cried his friend Akweley. Grandpa Nii, who was repairing a fishing net nearby, looked up. ‘The sea has been changing this shore for many years,’ he said. ‘But recently, the changes have worried us.’ Teye stared at the waves. Could something so beautiful also be so powerful?

Grandpa Nii, who was repairing a fishing net nearby, looked up.
‘The sea has been changing this shore for many years,’ he said.
‘But recently, the changes have worried us.’ Teye stared at the waves.
Could something so beautiful also be so powerful?
pages.alt: Teye and Akweley standing on a Ghanaian sandy beach looking at fallen wooden football goalposts near the rolling ocean waves while Grandpa Nii repairs a fishing net nearby.

pages.text: Grandpa Nii opened an old wooden box and brought out a photograph. It showed the same beach, but the coconut trees stood much farther from the water. ‘Was this really our village?’ Teye asked. ‘Yes. I took that photograph many years ago.’ Akweley compared it with the present shoreline. ‘Then the land has changed!’ Grandpa nodded. ‘Waves and currents can carry sand away from one place and deposit it somewhere else. This is part of coastal erosion.’ Teye repeated the new words slowly. ‘Coastal erosion. So the sea does not simply stay in one place?’ ‘Exactly,’ said Grandpa. ‘And different coasts change in different ways.’

pages.text: At school, their teacher, Madam Ofori, filled a shallow tray with sand and water. She shaped the sand into a little beach. ‘Watch carefully.’ She gently moved the water back and forth. Tiny grains of sand shifted. ‘The moving water carries sediment,’ she explained. ‘Along real coastlines, waves, currents, storms and changes in sea level can all affect the shore.’ Teye raised his hand. ‘Is climate change involved?’ ‘It can be,’ said Madam Ofori. ‘Rising sea levels can increase coastal risks. But we must investigate local conditions before deciding what causes changes at a particular beach.’

pages.text: That afternoon, Teye visited his friend Sena. Sena’s mother was moving belongings away from a wall near the beach. ‘The ground is getting too close to the water,’ she explained. ‘Will your family have to leave?’ Teye asked. ‘We are speaking with the local authorities and getting advice. We must make a safe decision.’ Teye felt worried. He had thought coastal erosion was only about sand and football. Now he understood that it could affect homes, livelihoods, roads and people’s safety.

pages.text: Some children suggested piling rubbish along the shore. ‘Plastic bags and old tyres might stop the waves!’ one boy declared. ‘Wait,’ Akweley said. ‘Wouldn’t that pollute the sea?’ Madam Ofori agreed. ‘An environmental problem should not be solved by creating another one. Protecting a coastline requires proper scientific assessment.’ She explained that suitable responses might include protecting coastal vegetation, planning where buildings are located, restoring beaches or constructing carefully designed coastal defences. ‘No single solution works everywhere,’ she added.

pages.alt: Akweley and Madam Ofori explaining to classmates why dumping plastic bags and tyres on the beach would pollute the sea and why scientific coastal solutions are needed.

pages.text: The class began a project called Our Changing Coast. They collected old photographs, interviewed residents and recorded observations from safe locations. A coastal scientist visited their school. ‘Your observations are useful,’ she told them. ‘But accurate measurements and long-term monitoring are needed before we can understand the changes.’ Teye asked whether the sea could ever be stopped completely. ‘We cannot control every wave,’ she replied. ‘But knowledge helps communities make better decisions.’

pages.text: At the community centre, the children presented their findings. They displayed photographs and explained what they had learned. Parents, fishers, engineers and local officials discussed safer building practices, waste management, monitoring and possible coastal protection measures. Teye was nervous when he stood to speak. ‘Our beach is more than a football field,’ he said. ‘It is part of our home. We need to protect people and the environment together.’ The room applauded.

pages.text: Weeks later, the children moved their football games to a safer field away from the shore. Teye still visited the beach with Grandpa Nii. One evening, the sunset painted the sea gold. ‘Grandpa, I cannot stop the ocean,’ he said. Grandpa smiled. ‘No, my boy. But you can learn about it, help people understand it and become someone who develops better solutions.’ Teye looked toward the horizon. ‘Then perhaps I will become a coastal engineer.’ ‘And I,’ said Akweley, arriving with her notebook, ‘will become the scientist who checks your calculations!’ They laughed as the waves rolled gently onto the sand.

activities.question: Why was Teye surprised when he arrived at the beach?
options: The shoreline had reached their football field.
activities.explanation: The wooden goalposts lay in the sand almost touching the waves because the shoreline had reached their football field.

activities.question: What did the tray experiment demonstrate?
options: Moving water can transport sand and change a shoreline.
Sand can never be moved by water.
Only storms can move grains of sand.
activities.explanation: Madam Ofori’s tray experiment showed that moving water can transport sand (sediment) and change the shape of a shoreline.

activities.question: Which of these can contribute to coastal change?
options: Waves, currents, storms or rising sea level
Playing football on an inland grass pitch
activities.explanation: Waves, currents, storms and rising sea level can all contribute to coastal change.

activities.definition: The wearing away or removal of material such as sand or soil from a coast
distractors: Planting coconut trees far inland on a hill
Repairing a fishing net with cotton thread

activities.question: Why is dumping rubbish on the beach a poor solution to coastal erosion?
options: It causes pollution and is not a properly designed defence.
It makes the ocean water too cold for fish.
It turns plastic bags into heavy rocks.
activities.explanation: Dumping rubbish causes pollution and does not provide a properly designed coastal defence.

activities.question: When comparing photographs of the same shoreline from different years, what should you remember?
options: Identify visible changes, but photos alone do not prove the cause.
One old photograph proves every cause without measurements.
Shorelines never change over many years.
activities.explanation: Photographs help us identify visible changes over time, while accurate measurements and monitoring are needed to establish causes.

activities.prompt: If you design a poster titled "Protect Our Coast", which message is most scientifically reasonable?
options: Keep beaches clean, protect coastal plants and follow expert advice.
Pile old tyres and plastic bags along the water.
Build houses right on the wet sand next to the waves.

activities.prompt: Put the events of Teye and Akweley’s coastal investigation in order.
items: Teye and Akweley find the sea has reached their beach goalposts.
Grandpa Nii shows an old photo and Madam Ofori runs a sand test.
The class rejects dumping rubbish and learns from a coastal scientist.
The children present their findings at the community meeting.

activities.prompt: How did Teye feel when he stood up at the community meeting to speak up for both people and the coastal environment?

glossary.definition: The line where a body of water meets the land or beach.
Steady flows of water moving in a particular direction in the sea.
The wearing away and removal of sand, soil or rock by water or wind.
Solid material such as sand or silt carried and deposited by water or wind.
The ways people earn the money or resources needed to support their families.
Plants and trees growing in a particular area, such as coastal grasses and mangroves.
Observing and measuring something regularly over a period of time.
